note: Existing-source, strict-license-screened public gallery. Additional historical photos remain held from this site. Anatomy overlays are teaching annotations, not a separate verified voucher determination.

tiles.heading: 01 · LOOK HERE FIRST
tiles.details: Begin with the photographed attached terminal cluster (panel 0): many narrow, one-sided racemes arise close together near one flowering-stem tip and appear pale and feathery. Flora of North America describes roughly 4–20 branches, usually about 5–10 cm long. Panel 3 shows the actual overlapping spikelet rows. A feathery head alone is NOT a secure species ID: inspect a mature detached fertile lemma for the distinctive distal tuft of long fine hairs, separate from its stiff awn. Panel 0 is a HEAD photograph, not a connected rooted plant. New panel 12 shows a species-determined flowering plant still growing in rocky El Paso roadside gravel with multiple upright culms. This is useful regional habitat and growth context, but its roots are hidden: do NOT call it a photographed rooted crown.
tiles.short: Pale feathery fan at one terminal hub; verify the hair crown
tiles.status: FEATHERY TERMINAL HEAD, ONE-SIDED SPIKELETS, REAL TEXAS IN-GROUND HABIT PICTURED; CONNECTED ROOT CROWN NOT EXPOSED

tiles.heading: 02 · GROWTH FORM AND TRUE LIGULE
tiles.details: Descriptions usually call this a tufted annual with ascending or bent lower stems, sometimes rooting at nodes. The existing ground-level photo (panel 6) shows basal culms converging, NOT exposed roots, independently rooted nodes or proof of lifespan. Panel 2 shows the correct blade/sheath junction but does NOT resolve the true free ligule. Flora of North America reports an erose/ciliate ligule up to about 4 mm, whereas a Southwest treatment describes approximately 0.2–1 mm; keep these treatment-specific values separate. Photograph the opened inner membrane beside a 1-mm ruler and the attached rooted base; do not label pale sheath lips as the ligule. NEW panels 10 and 11 now actually photograph the chestnut-red circumferential STEM NODE on green Chloris virgata culms. Panel 11 also shows the neighboring long green blade and sheath exterior. The dark node is a STEM JOINT, not the blade/sheath collar ligule. The photographic annotation arrows point only to the dark nodes; panel 12 shows a Texas plant in soil but DOES NOT expose or certify roots. The complete inner 0.2–4-mm treatment-variable free membrane still needs a measured face-on photograph.
tiles.short: Dark true stem nodes now photographed; true inner ligule and attached roots still need close-up
tiles.status: TRUE DARK STEM NODE PHOTOGRAPHED AND ARROWED; INNER MEMBRANOUS LIGULE / EXPOSED ROOTS STILL MISSING

tiles.heading: 03 · MEASURE MATURE SPIKELETS
tiles.details: On one mature unilateral raceme, examine several overlapping spikelets at 10–20×. Flora of North America and diagnostic disseminule treatments describe a spikelet roughly 2.5–4.5 mm long, with one bisexual fertile lower floret and one or sometimes two reduced sterile upper florets. Panels 1 and 3 show real attached units; panels 4, 5 and 7 show detached reproductive units. Do NOT confuse a detached floret unit with a whole spikelet or bare seed. A 0.5-mm scale and one opened same-voucher spikelet are still missing.
tiles.short: About 2.5–4.5 mm; one fertile plus reduced sterile florets
tiles.status: REAL ATTACHED AND DETACHED REPRODUCTIVE UNITS; CALIBRATED INTACT/DISSECTED SPIKELET MISSING

tiles.heading: 04 · SEPARATE BOTH GLUMES
tiles.details: The two basal glumes are unequal, keeled and generally one-veined in Flora of North America, Kew GrassBase and USDA diagnostic treatments. Published lower-glume length is approximately 1.5–2.5 mm and upper approximately 2.5–4.5 mm; the upper tip may taper to a bristlelike point, so do not make an absolute awnless-glume claim. Jim Conrad's panel 4 suggests persistent narrow glumes on the rachis, but no existing image separately measures both or proves each vein. Open a mature specimen and photograph each glume with transmitted light and millimeter scale.
tiles.short: Lower about 1.5–2.5 mm; upper about 2.5–4.5 mm
tiles.status: GLUME POSITION SUGGESTED IN PHOTOGRAPH; INDIVIDUAL GLUME LENGTH AND VENATION UNVERIFIED

tiles.heading: 05 · HAIR CROWN, FERTILE LEMMA AND TWO AWNS
tiles.details: A fertile lemma body is about 2.5–4 mm in Kew/AusGrass, usually three-veined, with a conspicuous distal fringe/crown of fine hairs approximately 1.5–4 mm. Its distinct subapical awn is reported about 2.5–15 mm in Flora of North America and 5–15 mm in GrassBase. The first sterile upper lemma is reduced (roughly 1.4–3 mm across treatments) and bears its OWN awn, commonly around 3–12 mm; a second very reduced sterile lemma may occur. Panels 5 and 7 genuinely show fine pale hair tufts and two stiff awn shafts, but do NOT resolve their separate attachment points or calibrated lengths. Add no anatomical insertion arrows without dissection.
tiles.short: Fine 1.5–4 mm crown hairs are NOT the stiff lemma awns
tiles.status: ACTUAL FINE HAIRS AND TWO AWNS VISIBLE; INDIVIDUAL LEMMA INSERTIONS AND MEASUREMENTS MISSING

tiles.heading: 06 · CENTRAL TEXAS LOOK-ALIKES
tiles.details: Compared with C. verticillata (OTHER SPECIES panel 9), feather fingergrass commonly crowds its pale feathery racemes near one terminal hub rather than separating long racemes into obvious stem tiers. C. cucullata has short crowded branches and a rounded swollen upper sterile lemma hood; C. andropogonoides has long, relatively slim radiating branches. The source-reported C. × subdolichostachya remains on its scientific hybrid voucher hold; neither parent image nor head silhouette certifies the hybrid. For a confident local ID compare an attached flowering axis, true ligule, paired glumes, fertile hair crown and both awn origins, not color or branch count alone. The new dark-node photos (panels 10–11) add real vegetative anatomy that can distinguish a stem node from the leaf collar; the Texas habitat panel 12 is only growth context, NOT taxonomic proof of lower rooting.
tiles.short: Tiered tumble windmillgrass; hooded windmillgrass; slim radiating windmills
tiles.status: LOOK-ALIKE LESSON READY; MATCHED LOCAL VOUCHER DISSECTIONS AND PUBLIC SITE QA MISSING

steps.title: 1 · First, recognize the plant
steps.look_for: FIRST recognize the pale FEATHERY cluster of narrow one-sided racemes arising close together at the tip of ONE flowering stem (commonly 4–20 branches in Flora of North America). THEN inspect an actual detached mature floret for the conspicuous distal tuft of fine fertile-lemma hairs and its separate awn. To compare with C. verticillata, look for separated head whorls; to compare with C. cucullata, dissect the inflated sterile hood. A head silhouette alone is not a certain species identification.
steps.why_it_matters: Start with the recorded recognition characters before making a species identification.

steps.title: 2 · Examine the whole plant
steps.look_for: Tufted annual grass of disturbed places with terminal digitate panicle; racemes often 5–10 cm.
steps.why_it_matters: Habit and growing context are supporting evidence, not proof of hidden roots or rhizomes.

steps.title: 3 · Inspect leaves, collar and nodes
steps.look_for: Descriptions usually call this a tufted annual with ascending or bent lower stems, sometimes rooting at nodes. The existing ground-level photo (panel 6) shows basal culms converging, NOT exposed roots, independently rooted nodes or proof of lifespan. Panel 2 shows the correct blade/sheath junction but does NOT resolve the true free ligule. Flora of North America reports an erose/ciliate ligule up to about 4 mm, whereas a Southwest treatment describes approximately 0.2–1 mm; keep these treatment-specific values separate. Photograph the opened inner membrane beside a 1-mm ruler and the attached rooted base; do not label pale sheath lips as the ligule. NEW panels 10 and 11 now actually photograph the chestnut-red circumferential STEM NODE on green Chloris virgata culms. Panel 11 also shows the neighboring long green blade and sheath exterior. The dark node is a STEM JOINT, not the blade/sheath collar ligule. The photographic annotation arrows point only to the dark nodes; panel 12 shows a Texas plant in soil but DOES NOT expose or certify roots. The complete inner 0.2–4-mm treatment-variable free membrane still needs a measured face-on photograph.
steps.why_it_matters: Examine the real structures; the photo may not expose or measure all the described characters.

steps.title: 4 · Check the flowering structure
steps.look_for: Fertile lemma about 2.5–4.2 mm, with long apical marginal hairs (>1.5 mm) and awn about 2.5–15 mm; one or two reduced sterile florets.
steps.why_it_matters: Use an attached, correctly identified specimen when deciding the flower or spikelet structures.

steps.title: 5 · Compare similar grasses
steps.look_for: C. virgata often has a single terminal digitate fan of feathery racemes, while verticillata has well-separated tiers and may form a tumbling mature head. C. cucullata has shorter crowded whorls and the strongly inflated sterile hood. Fertile-lemma apical hair crown, awn and annual crown are needed for confident C. virgata.
steps.why_it_matters: Confirm at least two independent botanical characters; do not remove a native candidate from color alone.

panels.label: FEATHERY ATTACHED HEAD — one compact terminal fan (not whole plant)
panels.caption: The photographed terminal Chloris virgata head has narrow feathery branches crowded together at its attachment region. The head is ATTACHED to a culm, but this photograph is not an entire rooted plant, not a view of lower nodes, and not a measured ligule or spikelet dissection. Contrast the general architecture with the separated flowering whorls of C. verticillata.
panels.creator: Matt Lavin
panels.annotation_note: Hays Botany displays overlaid numbered anatomy pointers; the source JPEG itself is unchanged.

panels.label: BLADE–SHEATH JUNCTION — collar location visible, ligule free edge unresolved
panels.caption: The two pale split sheath lips and rising green blade are clearly photographed; look at the INNER blade/sheath junction between them for the true ligule. Fine pale strands near the rim are present but must NOT be labeled as a measured free ligule. Flora accounts describe an erose/ciliate or ciliolate membranous ligule: Southwest treatment about 0.2–1 mm; FNA reports to 4 mm across plants; AusGrass gives ~0.8 mm. Do not force a single 0.2–1 mm limit on every specimen. Photograph an opened junction side-on and face-on beside a true 1-mm ruler.
panels.creator: Harry Rose (Macleay Grass Man)
panels.annotation_note: Hays Botany displays overlaid numbered anatomy pointers; the source JPEG itself is unchanged.

panels.label: 4 · One-sided rows of actual spikelets on a raceme
panels.caption: Follow the two tightly packed spikelet rows along ONE side of this raceme. Long pale projections are visible, but this photo alone cannot distinguish the fertile lemma's hair crown from the separate fertile and sterile awns. Finger is not a millimeter ruler.
panels.creator: Harry Rose (Macleay Grass Man)
panels.annotation_note: Hays Botany displays overlaid numbered anatomy pointers; the source JPEG itself is unchanged.

markers.label: Two one-sided rows of attached spikelets

panels.label: LOOSE FLORET UNITS — long awns and persistent glumes
panels.caption: Jim Conrad's original 2024 Mexico photograph shows shed two-awned reproductive UNITS at left and a still-attached spikelet-bearing raceme at right. Persistent narrow glumes remain along the rachis while the florets separate; use the fine white hair tufts and long awns as gross clues. No calibrated ruler and no independently traced fertile-versus-sterile lemma origins.
panels.creator: Jim Conrad
panels.modifications: Reencoded RGB JPEG, EXIF removed; browser annotations as separate markup only

panels.label: FLORET MACRO — two awns and distinctive pale hair crown
panels.caption: Jim Conrad identifies the larger fertile and attached smaller sterile floret in this true macro. Clearly visible: TWO projecting long awns, a pale seed-enclosing body and a dense spray of white hairlike structures beside its apex. These white hairs agree with the diagnostic fertile-lemma hair crown, but the photograph lacks a ruler and individual awn insertion sites are not independently resolved. Original Mexico specimen, not a Hays voucher.
panels.creator: Jim Conrad

panels.label: GROUND-LEVEL GROWTH — converging basal culms, roots hidden
panels.caption: Jim Conrad's original photograph shows grass culms radiating from an obscured central base in dry Mexican reservoir soil. The fingertip indicates scale and draws attention to the culm-convergence region. NO underground roots, stolon-root connection, separate rooted node or perennial rhizome is actually visible. Flora descriptions generally call this a tufted annual, sometimes rooting along prostrate stems; a single photograph cannot prove lifespan.

panels.label: 5 · Detached spikelet — long awns and fine apical hairs
panels.caption: Harry Rose's detached C. virgata spikelet shows two conspicuous long brown awns and a separate fan of fine, pale hairs near the floret tip. The arrows point only to an actual awn shaft and visible fine hairs. The photographed hair tuft agrees with published descriptions of the fertile lemma's subapical hair crown, but this view lacks a ruler and does NOT independently resolve which awn belongs to which fertile/sterile lemma, glume outlines, or exact lengths. Australian source-identified specimen, not a Hays County voucher.
panels.creator: Harry Rose (Macleay Grass Man)
panels.modifications: Archived JPEG resized from original; original image unchanged by new arrows (browser overlay only).

panels.label: 6 · Young detached spikelet — emerging hairs
panels.caption: Harry Rose's young source-labelled C. virgata spikelet shows pale enclosing parts and a fan of long fine hairs projecting upward from near the central floret tip. The arrow identifies only the visible hair tuft; the individual glumes, fertile versus sterile lemma, and attachment points of the long awns cannot be independently traced at this angle. The original photographer calls the spikelet young; this Australian photo is not a Texas voucher.

panels.caption: TUMBLE WINDMILLGRASS, NOT FEATHER FINGERGRASS: Douglas Goldman's source-verified CC BY-SA 4.0 macro shows individual awned units along a narrow one-sided branch. Compare with the C. virgata separately source-photographed fluffy long-hair crown; do not infer a species from presence of awns alone.

panels.label: TRUE CULM NODE — photographed dark circumferential joint
panels.caption: A real dark chestnut-red STEM NODE encircles the otherwise green grass culm, above a finger for general size. The node forms a joint on the stem; it is NOT a true free ligule and proves neither rooting at the lower node nor the plant's lifespan.

markers.label: Dark true stem node (not a ligule)

panels.label: NODE VERSUS LEAF BLADE — dark joint and attached green outer sheath
panels.caption: An actual reddish node ring crosses the upright green stem; a separate long leaf blade diverges nearby. The two are NOT interchangeable: the node is a stem joint, while the free LIGULE lies inside the blade/sheath transition and cannot be resolved here. Long bright hairlike filaments in the background are not identified as the ligule.

intro: FIRST recognize the pale FEATHERY cluster of narrow one-sided racemes arising close together at the tip of ONE flowering stem (commonly 4–20 branches in Flora of North America). memory_rule: Start with the striking densely grouped pale terminal fan in the first picture; the branches rise together near the top.
safety_note: Field-ID and photo-rights review verified existing archived images and gross arrows. The 9 archived JPEGs include an attached head, actual floret macros, a ground-level base with roots HIDDEN, and a collar search view with unmeasured ligule. Do not count the head image as a whole rooted plant, and do not call the sheath lip a ligule or infer root emergence at a basal node. Zero new image bytes/arrows in this pass.
field_rule: C. virgata often has a single terminal digitate fan of feathery racemes, while verticillata has well-separated tiers and may form a tumbling mature head. C. cucullata has shorter crowded whorls and the strongly inflated sterile hood. Fertile-lemma apical hair crown, awn and annual crown are needed for confident C. virgata.
photo_data_caution: Missing or restricted comparison photographs have not been replaced by guesses. Source statements are not proof the associated structure is visible in any available photo.

morphology.habit: Tufted annual grass of disturbed places with terminal digitate panicle; racemes often 5–10 cm.
morphology.spikelets: Fertile lemma about 2.5–4.2 mm, with long apical marginal hairs (>1.5 mm) and awn about 2.5–15 mm; one or two reduced sterile florets.
